title: French grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday French, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is French as it is spoken in France today.

units.title: Your day and the people in it

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name, your nationality and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first French conversation.
lessons.topic: {{je m'appelle}} “my name is”, {{je suis}} “I am”; nationalities for a man and a woman; {{et vous ?}}

goal.t: Bonjour, je m'appelle Emma. Je suis américaine.
goal.tr: Hello, my name is Emma. I'm American.

dialog.tr: Hello! My name is Thomas.
Hello, my name is Emma.
Are you English?

dialog.t: Non, je suis américaine. Je suis de Chicago. Et vous ?
dialog.tr: No, I'm American. I'm from Chicago. And you?

dialog.t: Moi, je suis français. Je suis de Lyon.
dialog.tr: Me, I'm French. I'm from Lyon.
Nice to meet you!
Nice to meet you!

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: I'm from Lyon.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she, it.

blocks.p: **Saying who you are.** {{Je m'appelle…}} is “my name is…” (word for word, “I call myself…”). {{Je suis…}} is “I am…”: {{je suis américaine}} “I'm American”, {{je suis de Lyon}} “I'm from Lyon”. {{De}} is “from”.

**I is je.** “I” is {{je}}, with a small letter (English “I” is always a capital; French {{je}} isn't). Before a vowel, the {{e}} drops and an apostrophe takes its place: {{je m'appelle}} is {{je}} + {{me}} “myself” + {{appelle}}.

**Men and women.** Words that say what someone is often change for a woman. Usually you add {{-e}}: Emma says {{je suis américaine}}; Thomas would say {{je suis américain}}. When the word ends in a consonant, the {{-e}} makes you hear it: {{français}} ends in a silent {{s}}, but in {{française}} you hear a “z” sound.
**And you?** {{Et vous ?}} turns the question back to the other person. {{Vous}} is the polite “you”, for someone you don't know yet. The next lesson shows the friendly one, {{tu}}.

ex.note: no word for “a” before a job (lesson 4)
to a woman: a question just by raising your voice
adding {{monsieur}} or {{madame}} is polite, not stiff

blocks.tip: Nationalities take a small letter in French: {{je suis anglais}}. Say {{bonjour}} all day, and {{bonsoir}} “good evening” from about six o'clock.

mistakes.why: {{Je m'appelle}} already means “my name is”: there is no “is” to add.
After {{je suis}}, a nationality takes a small letter.

lessons.title: Ask how someone is, politely or as a friend
lessons.summary: Ask “How are you?” and answer it, choosing {{tu}} for a friend and {{vous}} for everyone else.

goal.t: Salut, ça va ? — Ça va bien, et toi ?
goal.tr: Hi, how are you? — I'm fine, and you?

dialog.tr: Hi, Hugo! How's it going?

dialog.t: Ça va bien, merci. Et toi ?
dialog.tr: Fine, thanks. And you?
Meh, I'm tired.
Me too!

blocks.p: **Two ways to say “you”.** Léa and Hugo are friends, so they say {{tu}} to each other ({{toi}} when the word stands alone: {{et toi ?}}). With someone you don't know, French uses {{vous}}. The greeting changes with it.

dialog.tr: Hello, Mr. Dubois. How are you?
Very well, thank you. And you?
Fine, thanks.

blocks.means: polite and careful, for people you don't know well, older people, at work. Its opposite is informal: relaxed, for friends and family.

table: a friend, family, a child, a pet
someone you don't know, an older person, a colleague, a shop assistant

blocks.p: When in doubt, say {{vous}}: it is never rude. Young people switch to {{tu}} with each other at once; with anyone else, wait until they ask {{On peut se tutoyer ?}} “Shall we say tu?”. And {{vous}} is also “you” to several people, friends or not: {{Vous allez bien, les enfants ?}} “Are you all right, kids?”.

**Moi, toi.** {{Moi}} “me” and {{toi}} “you” are the forms that stand alone: {{Et toi ?}}, {{Moi aussi.}} “Me too.” The French also put {{moi}} in front of {{je}} to say “as for me”: {{Moi, je suis fatigué.}}

ex.note: {{ça va}} is both the question and the answer
word for word “I go very well”

blocks.tip: Answers to {{Ça va ?}}, from good to bad: {{Très bien !}}, {{Ça va bien.}}, {{Ça va.}}, {{Pas mal.}}, {{Bof.}}, {{Pas terrible.}} The French really do say {{bof}} when things are just so-so.

mistakes.why: Standing alone, “you” is {{toi}} (or {{vous}}), never {{tu}}.
To say how you are, French uses “go”: {{je vais bien}}. {{Je suis bien}} means “I'm comfortable”.
{{Salut}} is for friends. To someone you call {{madame}}, say {{bonjour}} and {{vous}}.

lessons.title: Ask for things politely
lessons.summary: Order a coffee, buy a ticket, ask for a room: {{je voudrais}}, and the first thing to know about French nouns, their gender.
lessons.topic: {{je voudrais}} + {{un}} or {{une}}; masculine and feminine nouns

goal.t: Je voudrais un café et une baguette, s'il vous plaît.
goal.tr: I'd like a coffee and a baguette, please.

dialog.tr: Hello, madam. What would you like?

dialog.t: Bonjour. Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
dialog.tr: Hello. I'd like a coffee, please.
One coffee. Anything else?

dialog.t: Et un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
dialog.tr: And a croissant, please.
Very good, madam.

blocks.p: **Asking politely.** {{Je voudrais}} is “I would like”. It is the polite way to ask for anything, in a café, a shop, a hotel or a station: {{je voudrais}}, the thing you want, then {{s'il vous plaît}}.

blocks.means: a word for a thing, a person, a place or an idea: coffee, ticket, friend, Paris, love.
in French, every noun is either masculine or feminine, things included: {{café}} is masculine, {{baguette}} is feminine. That is the noun's gender.
a little word in front of a noun: “a” and “the” in English. In French it also shows the noun's gender: {{un}}, {{une}}.

blocks.p: **Un or une?** “A” is {{un}} before a masculine noun and {{une}} before a feminine one. The gender belongs to the word, not to the thing: there's nothing feminine about a table, but it's {{une table}}.

table: {{une bouteille d'eau}} a bottle of water

blocks.p: **Learn each noun with its un or une.** There are hints (most nouns ending in {{-tion}}, {{-té}} or {{-ette}} are feminine; most ending in {{-ment}} or {{-eau}} are masculine), but the surest way is to learn {{une chambre}}, not just {{chambre}}.

ex.t: Je voudrais un thé, s'il vous plaît.
Je voudrais une chambre pour deux nuits.
ex.tr: I'd like a room for two nights.

ex.t: Je voudrais un billet pour Paris.
ex.tr: I'd like a ticket to Paris.
I'd like a bottle of water.

ex.note: short, and fine at a counter

ex.t: Je voudrais l'addition, s'il vous plaît.
ex.tr: Could I have the check, please?

blocks.tip: {{Un}} and {{une}} also mean “one”: {{un café}} is “a coffee” or “one coffee”, {{une nuit}} “one night”.

mistakes.why: {{Bière}} is feminine, so it's {{une}}.

mistakes.right: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
mistakes.why: {{Je veux}} “I want” sounds rude when you ask for something. Say {{je voudrais}}.

lessons.title: Talk about other people
lessons.summary: Introduce a friend, say where people are from and what they do: all of {{être}} “to be”.
lessons.topic: {{être}}: {{je suis, tu es, il est…}}; {{il}}, {{elle}}, {{ils}}, {{elles}}; jobs without “a”; {{c'est}} or {{il est}}

goal.t: Voici Marc. C'est mon ami. Il est médecin.
goal.tr: This is Marc. He's my friend. He's a doctor.

dialog.t: Paul, voici Marc et Sophie. Ils sont de Bordeaux.
dialog.tr: Paul, this is Marc and Sophie. They're from Bordeaux.
Hello! Are you on vacation?

dialog.t: Non, nous sommes ici pour le travail. Je suis infirmière et Marc est médecin.
dialog.tr: No, we're here for work. I'm a nurse and Marc is a doctor.
Oh, that's great!

blocks.means: a word for an action or a state: eat, go, have, be.
who or what the sentence is about, usually just before the verb: **Marc** is a doctor; **we** are here.
to give a verb the form that goes with its subject: {{je suis}}, {{tu es}}, {{il est}}. All these forms together are the verb's conjugation.

blocks.p: **One verb, many forms.** “To be” is {{être}}. Like most French verbs, it changes with its subject. English does this a little (I am, he is); French has a form for almost every person.
**He, she, they.** {{Il}} is “he”, {{elle}} is “she”. For “they”, French chooses too: {{elles}} for a group of women only, {{ils}} for men, and for any mixed group (even one man among ten women).

**Jobs without “a”.** After {{je suis}}, {{il est}} and the rest, a job has no article: {{Il est médecin.}} “He's a doctor.” Like nationalities, many jobs change for a woman: {{étudiant}}, {{étudiante}}; {{infirmier}}, {{infirmière}}.

**C'est or il est?** To present someone, use {{c'est}} “this is, he is, she is” before a name, or before a noun with its article: {{C'est Marc.}} {{C'est mon ami.}} {{C'est un bon médecin.}} Use {{il est}} or {{elle est}} before a job, a nationality or a description standing alone: {{Il est médecin.}} {{Elle est sympa.}}

ex.tr: This is Sophie. She's a nurse.

blocks.tip: {{Vous êtes}} is said “voo-zet”: the {{s}} at the end of {{vous}}, normally silent, is heard as a “z” before a vowel. This joining is called liaison. The {{t}} in {{c'est un}} does it too: “say-tun”.

mistakes.why: After {{il est}}, a job has no {{un}} or {{une}}. (With {{c'est}} it needs one: {{C'est un médecin.}})
Before a name, say {{c'est}}.
A group of women only is {{elles}}.

practice.q: Three women and one man. “They” is…
practice.why: One man in the group is enough for {{ils}}.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
Choose the missing word.

lessons.title: Say what you have, your age and how you feel
lessons.summary: Talk about your family, say how old you are and that you're hungry or cold: with {{avoir}} “to have”, where English says “be”.
lessons.topic: {{avoir}}: {{j'ai, tu as, il a…}}; {{j'ai 30 ans}}; {{j'ai faim}}, {{j'ai froid}}

goal.t: J'ai trente ans et j'ai deux enfants.
goal.tr: I'm thirty and I have two children.

dialog.t: Tu as des frères et sœurs ?
dialog.tr: Do you have brothers and sisters?

dialog.t: Oui, j'ai une sœur. Elle a vingt ans.
dialog.tr: Yes, I have a sister. She's twenty.

dialog.t: Et toi, tu as quel âge ?
dialog.tr: And how old are you?
I'm twenty-five.
Me too! Are you hungry?
Yes, I'm really hungry!

blocks.p: **Having.** {{Avoir}} is “to have”. Like {{être}}, it changes with its subject. With {{je}}, it's {{j'ai}}: {{je}} loses its {{e}} before a vowel.
Listen for the difference between {{ils ont}} “they have” and {{ils sont}} “they are”: in {{ils ont}} you hear a “z” (“eel-zon”), in {{ils sont}} an “s” (“eel-son”).

**Your age is something you have.** French says “I have thirty years”: {{J'ai trente ans.}} The word {{ans}} “years” is never left out. To ask: {{Tu as quel âge ?}} or, politely, {{Vous avez quel âge ?}}
**Feelings you have.** Where English says “I am hungry”, French says “I have hunger”: {{J'ai faim.}} It's the same for thirst, cold, heat, fear, sleepiness, and for being right.

ex.t: Vous avez une chambre pour ce soir ?
ex.tr: Do you have a room for tonight?

blocks.tip: Numbers for ages: {{dix}} 10, {{vingt}} 20, {{trente}} 30, {{quarante}} 40, {{cinquante}} 50, {{soixante}} 60. Add the units with a dash: {{vingt-cinq}} 25, {{trente-huit}} 38 (lesson 12 has them all).

mistakes.why: Age is something you have: {{j'ai}}, with the word {{ans}}.
The word {{ans}} “years” must be said.
Hunger, thirst, cold, heat and fear are things you have: {{avoir}}.

lessons.title: Say no and what isn't so
lessons.summary: Say what you're not, what you don't have and that you don't understand: {{ne … pas}} around the verb.
lessons.topic: {{ne … pas}}; {{n'}} before a vowel; {{pas de}} after a negative

dialog.tr: Are you English?

dialog.t: Non, je ne suis pas anglaise, je suis américaine.
dialog.tr: No, I'm not English, I'm American.
Do you have a bag?

dialog.t: Non, je n'ai pas de sac.
dialog.tr: No, I don't have a bag.

dialog.t: Pas de problème, voilà un sac.
dialog.tr: No problem, here's a bag.

blocks.means: a sentence that says something is not so: I'm not English; I don't have a bag.

blocks.p: **Two pieces around the verb.** French puts {{ne}} before the verb and {{pas}} after it, like the bread of a sandwich: {{je suis}} → {{je ne suis pas}}. Before a vowel, {{ne}} becomes {{n'}}: {{j'ai}} → {{je n'ai pas}}.
**No “do”.** English adds “do” to say no (“I **don't** understand”). French doesn't: just {{ne … pas}} around the verb itself.

**Un and une become de.** After a negative, “a” ({{un}}, {{une}}) becomes {{de}}, or {{d'}} before a vowel: {{J'ai un sac.}} → {{Je n'ai pas de sac.}} “I don't have a bag.” But after {{être}} they stay: {{Ce n'est pas un problème.}} “It's not a problem.”

ex.t: Nous n'avons pas de chambre pour ce soir.
ex.tr: We don't have a room for tonight.

ex.note: word for word “it isn't serious”: you'll hear it every day

blocks.tip: In everyday speech the French often drop {{ne}}: {{C'est pas grave.}} {{Je sais pas.}} “I dunno.” You'll hear it everywhere. In writing, and while you learn, keep {{ne}}.

mistakes.why: {{Ne}} alone isn't enough: {{pas}} goes after the verb.
After a negative, {{un}} and {{une}} become {{de}}.
The verb goes between {{ne}} and {{pas}}.

lessons.title: Ask questions
lessons.summary: Ask yes-or-no questions in three ways, and ask where, when, how, how much, who, what and why.
lessons.topic: questions with the voice, with {{est-ce que}} and with question words; {{quel}}; inversion to recognise

goal.t: Excusez-moi, où est la gare, s'il vous plaît ?
goal.tr: Excuse me, where's the train station, please?

dialog.t: Excusez-moi, est-ce que vous parlez anglais ?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, do you speak English?

dialog.t: Un peu. Qu'est-ce que vous cherchez ?
dialog.tr: A little. What are you looking for?

dialog.t: Où est la gare, s'il vous plaît ?
dialog.tr: Where's the station, please?

dialog.t: C'est tout droit, à cinq minutes.
dialog.tr: It's straight ahead, five minutes away.
Thank you very much!
You're welcome!

blocks.p: **Yes-or-no questions: three ways.** Take any sentence, {{Vous parlez anglais.}} “You speak English.”, and…

table: raise your voice at the end (everyday speech)
put {{est-ce que}} in front (everyday, a little more careful)
swap the verb and the pronoun, with a dash (formal, written)

blocks.p: The first two are what you'll say. The third, called inversion, is what you'll read, and hear in formal situations: recognise it for now. {{Est-ce que}} becomes {{est-ce qu'}} before a vowel: {{Est-ce qu'il est là ?}} “Is he here?”

blocks.means: a word that asks for information: where, when, how, who, what, why.

blocks.p: **Where the question word goes.** In everyday French it can come first, or go at the end, where the answer would be: {{Où est la gare ?}} or {{La gare est où ?}}. After a question word at the start you can add {{est-ce que}}: {{Quand est-ce que tu arrives ?}}

**Which? What?** Before a noun, “what” or “which” is {{quel}}. It changes like the words in lesson 1: {{quel}} (masculine), {{quelle}} (feminine), {{quels}}, {{quelles}} (more than one). All four sound the same: {{Quelle heure est-il ?}} “What time is it?”, {{Tu as quel âge ?}} “How old are you?”

ex.t: Où sont les toilettes, s'il vous plaît ?

ex.note: to a friend; politely: {{Comment vous appelez-vous ?}}

ex.t: Pourquoi ? — Parce que je suis fatigué.

blocks.tip: To answer “yes” to a negative question, French has a special word: {{si}}. {{Tu n'as pas faim ? — Si !}} “Aren't you hungry? — Yes, I am!” A plain {{oui}} would sound odd here.

mistakes.why: For age, ask “what age” ({{quel âge}}), with {{avoir}}.

mistakes.tr: Aren't you hungry? — Yes, I am!
mistakes.why: To say yes to a negative question, French says {{si}}.

practice.why: Verb first, then the pronoun, with a dash: that's inversion.

lessons.title: Point at things and name them
lessons.summary: Say what things are, “a” or “the”, one or more: {{c'est un cadeau}}, {{ce sont les clés}}.
lessons.topic: {{le, la, l', les}} and {{un, une, des}}; plurals; {{c'est}} and {{ce sont}}

goal.t: Qu'est-ce que c'est ? — C'est une crêpe, la spécialité de la maison !
goal.tr: What's this? — It's a crêpe, the house specialty!

dialog.tr: What's that?
It's a present for Marie.
And this?

dialog.t: Ce sont des chocolats. Les chocolats sont pour toi !
dialog.tr: They're chocolates. The chocolates are for you!
Oh, thank you!

blocks.p: **A or the.** As in English, “a” ({{un}}, {{une}}) is for something new, “the” for something you both know about. Sam says {{des chocolats}} “some chocolates”, then {{les chocolats}} “the chocolates”: the ones he has just mentioned.

blocks.means: more than one: books, children. One is singular.

blocks.p: **Plurals.** Most nouns add {{-s}} in the plural, as in English, but in French the {{s}} is silent: {{livre}} and {{livres}} sound the same. So you hear the plural in the article: {{le livre}} “luh”, {{les livres}} “lay”. Nouns ending in {{-eau}} add {{-x}}: {{un gâteau}}, {{des gâteaux}}.
**Des.** In the plural, English often says nothing (“They're chocolates”). French needs an article: {{Ce sont des chocolats.}}
**C'est, ce sont.** {{C'est…}} “it's, this is” for one thing, {{ce sont…}} “they're, these are” for more than one. In speech you'll often hear {{c'est}} for both.
**L'.** Before a vowel or a silent {{h}}, {{le}} and {{la}} shorten to {{l'}}: {{l'eau}} “the water”, {{l'hôtel}} “the hotel”. And {{les}} links to a vowel with a “z”: {{les amis}} “lay-zah-mee”.

ex.tr: Is this the train to Lyon?

ex.t: Ce sont des amis de Paris.

blocks.tip: Learn each noun with {{le}} or {{la}}, or {{un}} or {{une}}: {{l'}} and {{les}} hide the gender. {{L'hôtel}} doesn't tell you that hotel is masculine ({{un hôtel}}).

lessons.title: Describe people and things
lessons.summary: Say what something is like, big or small, new or old, red or blue: adjectives that agree with their noun and mostly come after it.
lessons.topic: adjectives: agreement ({{-e}}, {{-s}}); after the noun, except a few short ones ({{grand, petit, bon, beau, nouveau, vieux, jeune}}…)

goal.t: C'est une petite maison blanche avec un grand jardin.
goal.tr: It's a little white house with a big yard.

dialog.tr: What does your suitcase look like?
It's big and black.

dialog.t: Il y a beaucoup de valises noires…

dialog.t: Elle a un petit ruban rouge.

dialog.t: Ah ! Voilà une valise noire avec un ruban rouge.

blocks.means: a word that describes a noun: big, red, French, kind.
to take the form that matches another word. A French adjective takes the gender of its noun, and its number (one or more than one).

blocks.p: **Agreement.** Add {{-e}} for a feminine noun, {{-s}} for a plural, {{-es}} for both. As with nouns, the {{-s}} is silent; the {{-e}} lets you hear a final consonant: {{noir}} and {{noire}} sound the same, but {{petit}} “puh-tee” becomes {{petite}} “puh-teet”.

An adjective that already ends in {{-e}} doesn't add another: {{un sac rouge}}, {{une valise rouge}}. Some change more: {{blanc}} → {{blanche}}, {{bon}} → {{bonne}}, {{gentil}} → {{gentille}}, {{italien}} → {{italienne}}.

**After the noun, mostly.** French usually puts the adjective after the noun: {{une voiture rouge}} “a red car”, {{un film intéressant}} “an interesting movie”. Colors and nationalities always go after.

**A few short ones go before.** About ten very common adjectives come before the noun. They're about beauty, age, goodness and size: {{beau}} (beautiful), {{joli}} (pretty), {{jeune}} (young), {{vieux}} (old), {{nouveau}} (new), {{bon}} (good), {{mauvais}} (bad), {{grand}} (big, tall), {{petit}} (small).
**With être.** After {{être}}, the adjective agrees with the subject: {{Il est petit.}} {{Elle est petite.}} {{Ils sont contents.}}

blocks.tip: {{Beau}}, {{nouveau}} and {{vieux}} have their own feminine forms: {{belle}}, {{nouvelle}}, {{vieille}}. {{Une belle journée}} “a beautiful day”, {{une vieille voiture}} “an old car”.

mistakes.why: Colors go after the noun.
{{Maison}} is feminine, so the adjective is too: {{petite}}.
After {{être}}, the adjective agrees with the subject: feminine and plural, {{-es}}.

lessons.title: Say whose it is
lessons.summary: Talk about your family and your things: “my, your, his, her” in French, and {{de}} for “Paul's”.
lessons.topic: {{mon, ma, mes}}, {{ton, ta, tes}}, {{son, sa, ses}}, {{notre, votre, leur}}; {{la voiture de Paul}}

goal.t: Voici ma sœur et son mari. Et ce sont leurs enfants.
goal.tr: This is my sister and her husband. And these are their children.

dialog.tr: Is that your family?

dialog.t: Oui ! Voici mon père et ma mère.
dialog.tr: Yes! This is my father and my mother.

dialog.t: Et le garçon, c'est ton frère ?
dialog.tr: And the boy, is that your brother?

dialog.t: Non, c'est le fils de ma sœur. Il s'appelle Léo.
dialog.tr: No, it's my sister's son. His name is Léo.
He's cute!

blocks.means: a word that says whose something is: my, your, his, her, our, their.

blocks.p: **My, your…** “My” agrees with the thing you have, like an adjective: {{mon}} before a masculine noun, {{ma}} before a feminine one, {{mes}} before a plural.

**His or her: the same word.** {{Son}}, {{sa}} and {{ses}} mean “his” or “her”. They agree with the thing owned, not with the owner: {{sa mère}} is “his mother” or “her mother”, because {{mère}} is feminine; {{son père}} is “his father” or “her father”. The rest of the sentence tells you who.

**Before a vowel: mon.** Before a feminine word that starts with a vowel, {{ma}}, {{ta}} and {{sa}} become {{mon}}, {{ton}}, {{son}}, just to sound smooth: {{mon amie}} “my friend” (a woman), {{son école}} “his school, her school”.
**Paul's: la … de Paul.** French has no 's. Say “the car of Paul”: {{la voiture de Paul}}; {{le fils de ma sœur}} “my sister's son”.

ex.note: {{frère}} is masculine, so {{son}}, though Marie is a woman

ex.t: C'est la voiture de mon père.

blocks.tip: “Your” follows “you”: {{ton, ta, tes}} with someone you call {{tu}}, {{votre, vos}} with {{vous}}. At a hotel: {{Votre nom, s'il vous plaît ?}} “Your name, please?”

mistakes.why: {{Son}} and {{sa}} agree with the thing owned: {{frère}} is masculine.
Before a vowel, {{ma}} becomes {{mon}}.
French has no 's: {{la voiture de Paul}}.

practice.q: Julie is talking about her father. “Her father” is…

lessons.title: Say where things are
lessons.summary: Say what there is and where: {{il y a}} “there is, there are”, and “on, under, next to, opposite”, with {{du}} and {{au}}.
lessons.topic: {{il y a}}; {{dans, sur, sous, devant, derrière, entre, à côté de, près de, en face de}}; {{du}}, {{des}}, {{au}}, {{aux}}

goal.t: Il y a une pharmacie à côté de la gare.
goal.tr: There's a pharmacy next to the station.

dialog.t: Excusez-moi, il y a un supermarché près d'ici ?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, is there a supermarket near here?

dialog.t: Oui, il y a un supermarché en face du musée.
dialog.tr: Yes, there's a supermarket opposite the museum.

dialog.t: Et il y a des restaurants dans le quartier ?
dialog.tr: And are there restaurants in the neighborhood?

dialog.t: Oui, il y a beaucoup de restaurants à côté de la place.
dialog.tr: Yes, there are a lot of restaurants next to the square.
Thank you!

blocks.p: **There is, there are: il y a.** {{Il y a}} is both “there is” and “there are”: {{il y a une pharmacie}}, {{il y a des restaurants}}. To ask, raise your voice or start with {{est-ce qu'}}: {{Est-ce qu'il y a un bus ?}} To say no: {{il n'y a pas de…}}

blocks.means: a little word that shows where, when or how: on, under, in, with, to.
two words joined into one, like “do not” → “don't”. In French it isn't optional: {{de}} + {{le}} is always {{du}}.

blocks.p: **De + le = du.** The prepositions ending in {{de}} ({{à côté de}}, {{près de}}, {{en face de}}) join with {{le}} and {{les}}: {{de + le}} becomes {{du}}, {{de + les}} becomes {{des}}. With {{la}} and {{l'}}, nothing changes. {{À}} “at, in, to” joins the same way: {{au}}, {{aux}}.

ex.t: Les clés sont sur la table.
ex.tr: The keys are on the table.

ex.t: Le chat est sous le lit.
ex.tr: The cat is under the bed.

ex.t: Il y a un café en face du cinéma.
ex.tr: There's a café opposite the movie theater.

ex.t: La banque est entre la poste et la pharmacie.
ex.tr: The bank is between the post office and the pharmacy.

ex.t: Il n'y a pas de bus le dimanche.

blocks.tip: {{Il y a}} is said fast, almost “ya”: {{Y a un problème ?}} “Is there a problem?” And {{Qu'est-ce qu'il y a ?}} means “What's the matter?”

mistakes.why: {{De}} + {{le}} always becomes {{du}}.
{{À}} + {{le}} always becomes {{au}}.

mistakes.wrong: Il n'y a pas des bus.
mistakes.right: Il n'y a pas de bus.
mistakes.why: After a negative: {{de}}.

lessons.title: Ask how much and how many
lessons.summary: Ask the price, understand the answer and buy the right amount: numbers to 100, {{combien}}, and {{un kilo de}}.

goal.tr: How much does it cost? — Ninety-five euros.

dialog.tr: Good morning, madam! What would you like?

dialog.t: Je voudrais un kilo de tomates, s'il vous plaît.
dialog.tr: I'd like a kilo of tomatoes, please.
Here you go. Anything else?
Six eggs. How much is that?
That's four euros eighty.
Here's five euros.

dialog.t: Et vingt centimes. Merci, bonne journée !
dialog.tr: And twenty cents. Thank you, have a nice day!

blocks.p: **Asking the price.** {{C'est combien ?}} “How much is it?”, {{Ça coûte combien ?}} “How much does it cost?”, and at the checkout {{Ça fait combien ?}} “How much is that (all together)?”

table: {{un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix}}

blocks.p: **70, 80, 90.** From 60 on, French in France counts in twenties: 70 is “sixty-ten”, 80 “four twenties”, 90 “four twenties ten”. (In Belgium and Switzerland you'll hear {{septante}} and {{nonante}}, but not in France.)
**Prices.** The euros first, then the cents, usually without the word {{centimes}}: {{4,80 €}} is {{quatre euros quatre-vingts}}. French writes a comma where English writes a decimal point.

**How many: combien de.** Before a noun, “how much” or “how many” is {{combien de}}: {{Combien de personnes ?}} “How many people?” Amounts take {{de}} too, with no article: {{un kilo de tomates}}, {{un verre de vin}}, {{beaucoup de monde}} “a lot of people”, {{un peu de sucre}} “a little sugar”.

ex.t: C'est combien, le croissant ? — Un euro vingt.
ex.tr: How much is the croissant? — One euro twenty.

ex.t: Combien de personnes ? — Nous sommes quatre.
ex.tr: How many people? — There are four of us.

ex.t: Je voudrais deux kilos de pommes.
ex.tr: I'd like two kilos of apples.

ex.t: Un verre de vin rouge, s'il vous plaît.
ex.tr: A glass of red wine, please.

ex.t: Il y a beaucoup de monde !
ex.tr: There are a lot of people!

blocks.tip: {{Six}} and {{dix}} end in an “s” sound on their own, a “z” before a vowel ({{six euros}} “see-zeuro”), and nothing before a consonant ({{six pommes}} “see pom”).

mistakes.why: After an amount, just {{de}}, with no article.
Before a noun: {{combien de}}.
In France, 70 is {{soixante-dix}}. {{Septante}} is Belgian and Swiss.

lessons.title: Say what you do: work, home, languages
lessons.summary: Say where you live, where you work and what languages you speak: the present of -er verbs (nine French verbs in ten), and {{on}} “we”.
lessons.topic: the present of -er verbs ({{parler, habiter, travailler}}); silent endings; {{on}} for “we”

goal.t: J'habite à Lyon et je travaille dans une banque.
goal.tr: I live in Lyon and I work in a bank.

dialog.tr: Where do you live?

dialog.t: J'habite à Lyon, près de la gare. Et toi ?
dialog.tr: I live in Lyon, near the station. And you?
Me too! Do you work here?

dialog.t: Oui, je travaille dans une école. J'enseigne l'anglais.
dialog.tr: Yes, I work in a school. I teach English.
You speak French well!

dialog.t: Merci ! Mon mari est français, alors on parle français à la maison.
dialog.tr: Thanks! My husband is French, so we speak French at home.

blocks.means: the basic form of a verb, the one in the dictionary: “to speak”, {{parler}}. French infinitives end in {{-er}}, {{-ir}} or {{-re}}.

blocks.p: **Nine verbs in ten end in -er.** {{Parler}} “to speak”, {{habiter}} “to live”, {{travailler}} “to work”, {{aimer}} “to like”, {{regarder}} “to watch”… They all work the same way: take off {{-er}} and add the ending for each person.

**The good news: most endings are silent.** {{Parle}}, {{parles}} and {{parlent}} all sound exactly the same: “parl”. Only {{nous parlons}} and {{vous parlez}} sound different. So when you speak, an -er verb has three forms, not six.

**On, the everyday “we”.** {{On}} means “one, people”, but in speech the French use it for “we” all the time: {{On parle français.}} “We speak French.” It takes the same form as {{il}}. {{Nous}} is for writing and careful speech.

**One present for two in English.** {{Je travaille}} is both “I work” and “I'm working”: French has a single present. {{Je travaille.}} “I'm working (right now).” {{Je travaille le samedi.}} “I work on Saturdays.”

ex.t: Je parle anglais et un peu français.
ex.tr: I speak English and a little French.

ex.t: On regarde un film ce soir ?
ex.tr: Shall we watch a movie tonight?

blocks.tip: The {{-ent}} of a verb is never said: {{ils travaillent}} is “eel tra-vye”. But at the end of other words you do hear it, as a nasal “ahn”: {{souvent}} “often”, {{content}} “happy”.

mistakes.tr: I speak English. / I'm speaking English.
mistakes.why: There's no “am” before a French verb: {{je parle}} is both “I speak” and “I'm speaking”.
{{Je}} becomes {{j'}} before a vowel or a silent {{h}}.
“They” takes {{-ent}}, and it's silent. {{-ons}} goes with {{nous}}.

lessons.title: Say what you like and don't like
lessons.summary: Say what you love, like and can't stand, and what you like doing: {{aimer}} with {{le, la, les}}, and with a verb.
lessons.topic: {{aimer, adorer, détester, préférer}} + {{le, la, les}} for things in general; + infinitive; {{aimer bien}}

goal.t: J'adore le chocolat, mais je déteste le café.
goal.tr: I love chocolate, but I hate coffee.

dialog.tr: Do you like movies?

dialog.t: Oui, j'adore les films français. Et toi ?
dialog.tr: Yes, I love French movies. And you?

dialog.t: J'aime bien, mais je préfère le théâtre.
dialog.tr: I like them, but I prefer the theater.

dialog.t: Ah bon ? Moi, je n'aime pas beaucoup le théâtre…
dialog.tr: Really? I don't much like the theater…
Do you like dancing?
Yes, I love dancing!

blocks.p: **Things in general take “the”.** In English you like “coffee”, “cats”, “French movies”, with no article. French needs one, and when you mean a thing in general (coffee as such, cats as a whole), it's {{le, la, les}}: {{J'aime le café.}} {{J'adore les chats.}}
**Aimer bien is a little less than aimer.** With things, the two are close. With a person, careful: {{je t'aime}} is “I love you”, but {{je t'aime bien}} is only “I like you”.

**Liking doing something: + infinitive.** Put the second verb in its basic form: {{J'aime danser.}} “I like dancing.” {{Je déteste attendre.}} “I hate waiting.” Where English has “-ing”, French has the infinitive.
**No de here.** After {{ne … pas}}, {{le, la, les}} stay as they are (only {{un, une, des}} become {{de}}): {{Je n'aime pas le café.}}
**Préférer** changes its accent when the ending is silent: {{je préfère}}, {{tu préfères}}, {{il préfère}}, {{ils préfèrent}}, but {{nous préférons}}, {{vous préférez}}.

ex.t: Je préfère la mer à la montagne.
ex.tr: I prefer the sea to the mountains.

ex.t: Je n'aime pas travailler le dimanche.
ex.tr: I don't like working on Sundays.

blocks.tip: To agree: {{Moi aussi.}} “Me too.” To agree with a negative: {{Moi non plus.}} “Me neither.” To disagree: {{Pas moi !}} after a yes, {{Moi, si !}} after a no.

mistakes.why: French needs an article, and a thing in general takes {{le, la, les}}.
Only {{un, une, des}} become {{de}} after a negative. {{Le, la, les}} stay.

lessons.title: Order food and drink
lessons.summary: Order a meal, ask for water, say you don't eat meat: {{du, de la, des}} for “some”, with {{prendre}} and {{boire}}.
lessons.topic: the partitive {{du, de la, de l', des}}; {{pas de}}; {{prendre}}, {{boire}}

goal.t: Pour moi, du poulet avec des frites, et de l'eau, s'il vous plaît.
goal.tr: For me, chicken with fries, and some water, please.

dialog.tr: Have you decided?

dialog.t: Oui. Je prends le poulet avec des frites.
dialog.tr: Yes. I'll have the chicken with fries.
And to drink?

dialog.t: De l'eau, s'il vous plaît. Une carafe d'eau.
dialog.tr: Water, please. A jug of tap water.

dialog.t: Moi, je ne mange pas de viande. Il y a un plat végétarien ?
dialog.tr: I don't eat meat. Is there a vegetarian dish?
Yes, vegetable lasagna.

blocks.p: **Some: du, de la.** English often says nothing (“I'd like water”) or “some” (“Do you want some bread?”). French always needs an article. For an amount of something you don't count, like bread, water or cheese, it's {{du}} or {{de la}}: {{du pain}} “(some) bread”, {{de la confiture}} “(some) jam”.

blocks.means: the article for “some of” a thing: {{du}}, {{de la}}, {{de l'}}, and {{des}} for several things. It means an amount of it, not all of it and not one.

blocks.p: **Three articles, three meanings.** {{J'aime le fromage.}} “I like cheese” (in general: lesson 14). {{Je voudrais un fromage.}} “I'd like a cheese” (one whole cheese). {{Je mange du fromage.}} “I'm eating cheese” (some of it).
**After a negative: de.** Like {{un}} and {{une}}, {{du, de la, des}} become {{de}} (or {{d'}}) after a negative: {{Je ne mange pas de viande.}} “I don't eat meat.”

**Ordering: je prends.** In a café or a restaurant the French say {{je prends…}} “I'll have…” (word for word “I take”) or {{pour moi…}} “for me…”, as well as {{je voudrais}}. {{Prendre}} “to take, to have” and {{boire}} “to drink” are irregular:

ex.t: Je prends un café et un croissant.
ex.tr: I'll have a coffee and a croissant.

ex.t: Elle boit du thé le matin.
ex.tr: She drinks tea in the morning.

ex.t: Il y a de la soupe ce soir.

blocks.tip: Tap water is free in a French restaurant: ask for {{une carafe d'eau}}. And {{manger}} keeps an {{e}} before {{-ons}}, so the {{g}} stays soft: {{nous mangeons}}.

mistakes.why: French needs an article: “some water” is {{de l'eau}}.

mistakes.wrong: Je ne mange pas du poisson.
mistakes.right: Je ne mange pas de poisson.
mistakes.why: After a negative, {{du}} becomes {{de}}.
With {{aimer}}, you mean cheese in general: {{le}}.

lessons.title: Say where you're going and where you're from
lessons.summary: Say you're going to the market, to France or to a friend's place, or coming back from work: {{aller}} and {{venir}}, with {{au}}, {{en}} and {{chez}}.
lessons.topic: {{aller}}, {{venir}}; {{à}} and {{de}} with places; {{en France}}, {{au Canada}}, {{aux États-Unis}}; {{chez}}

goal.t: Je vais au marché, puis chez ma grand-mère.
goal.tr: I'm going to the market, then to my grandmother's.

dialog.tr: Hello! Where are you going?

dialog.t: Je vais à la poste, puis au supermarché. Et vous ?
dialog.tr: I'm going to the post office, then to the supermarket. And you?

dialog.t: Je viens du marché. Et ce week-end, je vais chez ma fille, à Nantes.
dialog.tr: I'm coming from the market. And this weekend I'm going to my daughter's, in Nantes.
Have a nice weekend!

blocks.p: **Aller and venir.** “To go” and “to come” are irregular, and among the most useful verbs in French:

**To a place: à.** “To” is {{à}}, and it joins with {{le}} and {{les}} as in lesson 11: {{je vais au cinéma}}, {{à la plage}}, {{à l'hôtel}}, {{aux toilettes}}. Before a city, just {{à}}: {{je vais à Paris}}.
**From a place: de.** “From” is {{de}}, which joins the same way: {{je viens du bureau}}, {{de la plage}}, {{de Paris}}. It's also how you say where you come from: {{Je viens de Chicago.}}

**Countries.** Feminine countries (most of those ending in {{-e}}) take {{en}}: {{en France}}, {{en Italie}}, {{en Espagne}}. Masculine ones take {{au}}: {{au Canada}}, {{au Japon}}, {{au Mexique}}. Plural ones take {{aux}}: {{aux États-Unis}}. The same word means “to” and “in”: {{Je vais en France.}} {{J'habite en France.}}

**To someone's place: chez.** {{Chez}} means “at the home of” or “to the home of”: {{chez ma grand-mère}}, {{chez Paul}}, {{chez moi}} “at my place, home”. Also for some professionals: {{chez le médecin}} “to the doctor's”.

ex.t: Tu vas où ? — Je vais au travail.
ex.tr: Where are you going? — I'm going to work.

ex.t: On va à la plage cet après-midi ?
ex.tr: Shall we go to the beach this afternoon?

ex.t: Nous allons en Italie en août.
ex.tr: We're going to Italy in August.

blocks.tip: {{Aller}} is also how the French ask how you are (lesson 2): {{Comment allez-vous ?}}, word for word “How are you going?”.

mistakes.why: {{À}} + {{le}} is always {{au}}.
A feminine country takes {{en}}.
To a person's home: {{chez}}.

practice.tr: Tonight I'm going to the movies.

lessons.title: Talk about your free time and the weather
lessons.summary: Say what you do on weekends, the sports and music you play, and what the weather's like: {{faire}}, {{jouer à}} and {{jouer de}}.
lessons.topic: {{faire}}; {{faire du sport}}, {{faire les courses}}; {{jouer au foot}}, {{jouer du piano}}; {{il fait beau}}, {{il pleut}}

goal.t: Le samedi, je fais du vélo, et le dimanche, je joue au tennis.
goal.tr: On Saturdays I go cycling, and on Sundays I play tennis.

dialog.t: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?
dialog.tr: What are you doing this weekend?

dialog.t: S'il fait beau, je fais une randonnée.
dialog.tr: If it's nice out, I'm going hiking.
And if it rains?

dialog.t: Je joue du piano et je fais le ménage !
dialog.tr: I play the piano and do the cleaning!

dialog.t: Moi, je joue au foot avec des amis. Tu viens ?
dialog.tr: I'm playing soccer with some friends. Are you coming?

blocks.p: **Faire: “do” and “make”.** {{Faire}} is everywhere in French: it covers both “do” and “make”, and a lot of activities. Its {{vous}} and {{ils}} forms are irregular: {{vous faites}} (never “faisez”), {{ils font}}.

**Sports and hobbies: faire du, de la.** They take {{faire}} and the partitive of lesson 15: {{faire du sport}}, {{du vélo}} (cycling), {{du yoga}}, {{de la natation}} (swimming), {{de la musique}}. Chores take {{faire}} with {{le, la, les}}: {{faire la cuisine}} (cook), {{faire le ménage}} (clean), {{faire les courses}} (do the grocery shopping).

**Playing: jouer à, jouer de.** A game or a sport: {{jouer à}}, joined to the article: {{jouer au foot}}, {{jouer aux cartes}}. A musical instrument: {{jouer de}}: {{jouer du piano}}, {{jouer de la guitare}}.

**The weather: il fait.** {{Il fait beau.}} “It's nice out.” {{Il fait chaud.}} “It's hot.” {{Il fait froid.}} “It's cold.” Rain and snow have their own verbs: {{il pleut}} “it's raining”, {{il neige}} “it's snowing”. To ask: {{Quel temps fait-il ?}} “What's the weather like?”

ex.t: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce soir ?
Je fais du yoga le matin.
ex.tr: I do yoga in the morning.

ex.t: Mon frère joue de la guitare.
Nous faisons les courses le samedi.
ex.tr: We do the grocery shopping on Saturdays.

ex.t: Il pleut, on reste à la maison.

blocks.tip: {{Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?}} can mean “What are you doing?” or “What do you do?”. To ask about someone's job, the French say {{Qu'est-ce que vous faites dans la vie ?}}, “What do you do in life?”.

mistakes.why: {{Faire}} is irregular: {{vous faites}}.
An instrument takes {{jouer de}}, and {{de}} + {{le}} = {{du}}.
The weather takes {{il fait}}.

lessons.title: Say when and how often
lessons.summary: Tell the time, say on which days and how often you do things, and what you never do: {{à huit heures}}, {{le lundi}}, {{souvent}}, {{ne … jamais}}.
lessons.topic: the time ({{il est … heures}}); {{lundi}} or {{le lundi}}; {{toujours, souvent, parfois}}; {{ne … jamais}}

goal.t: Le lundi, je commence à huit heures, mais je ne travaille jamais le week-end.
goal.tr: On Mondays I start at eight, but I never work on weekends.

dialog.tr: When are you free?

dialog.t: Le mardi et le jeudi, après dix-sept heures.
dialog.tr: On Tuesdays and Thursdays, after 5 p.m.

dialog.t: Jeudi à dix-huit heures, ça va ?
dialog.tr: Thursday at 6 p.m., is that OK?
Yes, perfect. See you Thursday!

blocks.p: **The time.** {{Quelle heure est-il ?}} “What time is it?” The answer is {{il est}}, the number and {{heures}}: {{Il est huit heures.}} The minutes come straight after: {{Il est huit heures dix.}} “It's 8:10.”

table: {{neuf heures moins le quart}} (nine less the quarter)

blocks.p: **The 24-hour clock.** Timetables, shops and appointments use it: {{dix-huit heures}} “6 p.m.”, {{vingt heures trente}} “8:30 p.m.”, written {{18 h}}, {{20 h 30}}. “At” a time is {{à}}: {{à huit heures}}.

**Days.** {{lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche}}, with small letters. One particular day takes no article: {{jeudi}} “on Thursday”. Every week takes {{le}}: {{le jeudi}} “on Thursdays”. The parts of the day work the same way: {{le matin}} “in the morning, every morning”, {{le soir}} “in the evening”.

blocks.means: a word that says how, when or how often: often, well, very, never.

blocks.p: **How often.** {{Toujours}} (always), {{souvent}} (often), {{parfois}} (sometimes) and {{rarement}} (rarely) go right after the verb: {{Je mange souvent au restaurant.}} “I often eat out.”

**Never: ne … jamais.** “Never” works like {{ne … pas}} (lesson 6), with {{jamais}} in place of {{pas}}: {{Je ne travaille jamais le dimanche.}} And like {{pas}}, it turns {{un, du, des}} into {{de}}: {{Il ne boit jamais de café.}}

ex.t: Il est dix heures et demie.
Le train part à quinze heures vingt.
Je fais les courses le samedi matin.
ex.tr: I do the grocery shopping on Saturday mornings.
Shall we have dinner together on Friday?
She often goes to the movies.

ex.t: Je ne mange jamais de viande.

blocks.tip: {{Quelle heure est-il ?}} is the textbook question. In the street you'll mostly hear {{Il est quelle heure ?}} or {{Vous avez l'heure ?}} “Do you have the time?”.

mistakes.why: No preposition before a day: {{lundi}}, or {{le lundi}} for every Monday.

mistakes.wrong: Je ne jamais travaille le dimanche.
mistakes.right: Je ne travaille jamais le dimanche.
mistakes.why: The verb goes between {{ne}} and {{jamais}}.
The word {{heures}} is always said.
